title: THE GOSPEL (PROTO-LUKE)
description:
This edition presents the gospel read in Marcion's church in the second century, the text its opponents called his Evangelion, reconstructed verse by verse from the writers who quote it. The working premise of the project is that this text is not an abridgement of canonical Luke but an earlier form of it, here called Proto-Luke. A second premise, that it comes from the Jewish-Christian circle of James the Just, is treated as a hypothesis: the chapter notes describe what the attested text contains and say where it supports that identification and where it does not.

The witnesses. Marcion's gospel survives only in quotation. The principal witnesses are Tertullian, Against Marcion, book 4 (c. 207), who works through the text in order, in Latin; and Epiphanius, Panarion 42 (c. 375), whose 78 scholia quote it in Greek and state where it lacked passages of canonical Luke. The Dialogue of Adamantius is used only where its Marcionite speaker quotes the gospel. Other Fathers (Origen, Hippolytus, Ephrem, Eznik) are cited where they bear on a verse. All of them were hostile. What they report the text to have contained is treated as evidence; what they say about why it was so ("Marcion cut it") is polemic and is not used.

How each verse is decided. Every verse of Luke 3–24 has a record in the apparatus (data/apparatus/luke_03.json to luke_24.json), with the witnesses quoted from their primary texts and a class: attested present; attested absent; unattested but probably absent (where a witness who works through that stretch of text would have used the verse against Marcion and does not cite it); or unattested and undetermined. Of the 1,017 verses of Luke 3–24, 485 are attested present, 143 attested absent, 44 probably absent and 345 undetermined. Attested verses are printed. Undetermined verses are printed only inside a paragraph that contains an attested verse, and are set in grey: they are the canonical text where the witnesses are silent, not attested text. Of the 708 verses printed, 223 are grey. Passages attested absent or probably absent are not printed, and each chapter's notes say what is missing and on whose evidence.

The wording. The Greek is that of Nestle–Aland, 27th edition, checked against the printed page. A reading of Marcion's text replaces it only where a witness attests it in its own words and the evidence makes it very likely: a Greek quotation, agreement of two witnesses, or a witness's habit of citation that rules out its own paraphrase. Where only Tertullian's Latin attests a reading and the Latin cannot render the Nestle–Aland Greek, the Greek is a retroversion, and the note says so. Weaker readings are recorded in the notes and do not change the text. Roth's graded reconstruction (2015) is the second judgement for every reading; where this edition departs from it, the reason is given.

The text before Marcion. The witnesses attest the text of Marcion's church; the edition aims at the text he received. On the premise that Marcion did not cut, the two differ at most in wording. The readings of Marcion's text that no independent manuscript of Luke shares were therefore tested against a reading of the whole attested text in its inner, correspondential sense (docs/research/correspondence; METHOD §11). A reading gives way only where it breaks that inner story and the witnesses to Marcion's text are themselves divided, with the earliest supporting canonical Luke. One reading met both conditions: at 18:19 the later copies read "God the Father", Tertullian only "God", and "except God alone" is printed. The same reading found no gap in the attested text that would require any passage it lacks.

What the witnesses show. The text began with the fifteenth year of Tiberius and Jesus' coming down to Capernaum (3:1; 4:31), and had no birth narratives (Luke 1–2). Passages the witnesses state were absent include the parable of the two sons (15:11–32), the entry into Jerusalem and the cleansing of the temple (19:29–46), the tenants of the vineyard (20:9–17), and "Today you will be with me in paradise" (23:43). Some readings are not those of canonical Luke: in the Lord's prayer a petition for the holy spirit stands in place of "hallowed be your name" (11:2); before Pilate the accusers add that Jesus is "destroying the law and the prophets" and "turning away the women and the children" (23:2); on the road to Emmaus the disciples are rebuked for not believing "all that he spoke to you", not "all that the prophets spoke" (24:25). Other passages that have been thought foreign to this text are attested in it: the cup of the covenant in Jesus' blood (22:20); and, after the resurrection, "See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself; for a spirit does not have bones as you see that I have" (24:39), followed by a request for food (24:41). The words "handle me and see" and "flesh and" were not in that verse.

Priority. The witnesses give no sign that the absences follow a single doctrine, and canonical Luke contains a seam where the shorter text does not (the Capernaum reference of 4:23, which in Marcion's order follows the visit to Capernaum). A stylometric test of the published editions of Marcion's gospel (docs/stylometry) finds Luke 1–2 and the genealogy distinct in style from the rest of Luke. Outside them it finds no measurable stylistic difference between the passages Marcion's text lacked and those it kept, so style alone does not decide the direction of change. Whether canonical Luke expanded this text, or both derive from a common original, is left open; the notes say what canonical Luke "has" or "lacks" rather than what it "added".

Translation. The English is translated from the printed Greek, including the readings of Marcion's text, and not revised from an existing English version. It says what the Greek says, without softening it or replacing it with the familiar church word. δοῦλος is "slave", ἄγγελος "messenger", μαθητής "learner", ἀπόστολος "emissary", πίστις "trust", μετάνοια "a change of mind", and ἀφίημι, said of sins, "let go", the verb used for leaving nets and releasing captives. μακάριος is "fortunate", kept apart from εὐλογέω, "bless". Ἰάκωβος is "Jacob", the name the Greek gives. Greek has no capitals, so titles are not capitalised: "the son of God", "the son of the human" (ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου), "lord" said to Jesus. Capitals are kept for God, the Father, and "the Lord" where κύριος stands for the divine name. Where English cannot follow the Greek, a translation note says what the Greek has. A fixed rendering is explained where it first occurs (METHOD §6). Jesus is named as in the Greek; ὁ χριστός is "the Anointed One"; ὁ ζῶν at 24:5 is "the Living One". The text is printed to 24:47, the last verse any witness cites.

Sources. Tertullian, Adversus Marcionem, ed. and trans. E. Evans (Oxford, 1972). Epiphanius, Panarion, ed. K. Holl, GCS 31 (Leipzig, 1922). Der Dialog des Adamantius, ed. W. H. van de Sande Bakhuyzen, GCS 4 (Leipzig, 1901). Novum Testamentum Graece, 27th ed. (Stuttgart, 1993). The SBL Greek New Testament (2010), as a machine-readable control. D. T. Roth, The Text of Marcion's Gospel (Leiden: Brill, 2015). A. von Harnack, Marcion: Das Evangelium vom fremden Gott, 2nd ed. (Leipzig, 1924). The method, the record of every decision and the corrections made to the previous edition are in docs/audit (METHOD.md, AUDIT_LOG.md).

chapters.title: Proto-Luke Chapter 1
chapters.preamble: The text opens with a date and an arrival. Epiphanius quotes its first words, "In the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar", and states that the birth narratives, the baptism and the genealogy were not in it (Pan. 42.11.4–5). Tertullian joins the date directly to the descent to Capernaum (Marc. 4.7.1). There is no preface, no John the Baptist preaching, no baptism, no genealogy and no temptation. Jesus enters the narrative as an adult teacher in the synagogue of a Galilean town. The order also differs from canonical Luke. Tertullian treats the exorcism at Capernaum before the visit to Nazareth, and the Nazareth scene presupposes it ("whatever we heard happened at Capernaum", 4:23). The Nazareth visit itself is short. It has no reading from Isaiah, no question about Joseph's son and no Elijah and Elisha sayings, and Jesus is driven out over a single proverb. Verses printed in grey are not cited by any witness but stand inside a passage the witnesses attest; the notes list what is absent and why.

verses.english: In the fifteenth year of the rule of Tiberius Caesar, while Pontius Pilate was governing Judea, and Herod was ruling Galilee as tetrarch, and Philip his brother was ruling as tetrarch the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias was ruling Abilene as tetrarch,
verses.greek: Ἐν ἔτει πεντεκαιδεκάτῳ τῆς ἡγεμονίας Τιβερίου Καίσαρος, ἡγεμονεύοντος Ποντίου Πιλάτου τῆς Ἰουδαίας, καὶ τετρααρχοῦντος τῆς Γαλιλαίας Ἡρῴδου, Φιλίππου δὲ τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ αὐτοῦ τετρααρχοῦντος τῆς Ἰτουραίας καὶ Τραχωνίτιδος χώρας, καὶ Λυσανίου τῆς Ἀβιληνῆς τετρααρχοῦντος,

verses.english: he came down to Capernaum, a city of Galilee. And he was teaching them on the sabbaths.
verses.greek: κατῆλθεν εἰς Καφαρναοὺμ πόλιν τῆς Γαλιλαίας. καὶ ἦν διδάσκων αὐτοὺς ἐν τοῖς σάββασιν·

verses.english: And they were astounded at his teaching, because his word was with authority.
verses.greek: καὶ ἐξεπλήσσοντο ἐπὶ τῇ διδαχῇ αὐτοῦ, ὅτι ἐν ἐξουσίᾳ ἦν ὁ λόγος αὐτοῦ.

verses.english: And in the assembly there was a person having a spirit of an unclean daimon, and he cried out with a loud voice,
verses.greek: καὶ ἐν τῇ συναγωγῇ ἦν ἄνθρωπος ἔχων πνεῦμα δαιμονίου ἀκαθάρτου, καὶ ἀνέκραξεν φωνῇ μεγάλῃ·

verses.english: "Ah! What is there between us and you, Jesus, Nazarene? Did you come to destroy us? I know you, who you are: the holy one of God."
verses.greek: Ἔα, τί ἡμῖν καὶ σοί, Ἰησοῦ Ναζαρηνέ; ἦλθες ἀπολέσαι ἡμᾶς; οἶδά σε τίς εἶ, ὁ ἅγιος τοῦ θεοῦ.

verses.english: And Jesus rebuked it, saying, "Be muzzled, and go out from him." And the daimon, having thrown him into the middle, went out from him, having harmed him in nothing.
verses.greek: καὶ ἐπετίμησεν αὐτῷ ὁ Ἰησοῦς λέγων· Φιμώθητι καὶ ἔξελθε ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ. καὶ ῥίψαν αὐτὸν τὸ δαιμόνιον εἰς τὸ μέσον ἐξῆλθεν ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ μηδὲν βλάψαν αὐτόν.

verses.english: And astonishment came upon all, and they were talking with one another, saying, "What is this word, that with authority and power he gives orders to the unclean spirits, and they go out?"
verses.greek: καὶ ἐγένετο θάμβος ἐπὶ πάντας, καὶ συνελάλουν πρὸς ἀλλήλους λέγοντες· Τίς ὁ λόγος οὗτος ὅτι ἐν ἐξουσίᾳ καὶ δυνάμει ἐπιτάσσει τοῖς ἀκαθάρτοις πνεύμασιν, καὶ ἐξέρχονται;

verses.english: And the sound of him was going out into every place of the surrounding region.
verses.greek: καὶ ἐξεπορεύετο ἦχος περὶ αὐτοῦ εἰς πάντα τόπον τῆς περιχώρου.

verses.english: And he came to Nazara, where he had been brought up, and he went in, according to his custom, on the day of the sabbaths into the assembly, and stood up to read.
verses.greek: Καὶ ἦλθεν εἰς Ναζαρά, οὗ ἦν τεθραμμένος, καὶ εἰσῆλθεν κατὰ τὸ εἰωθὸς αὐτῷ ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῶν σαββάτων εἰς τὴν συναγωγήν, καὶ ἀνέστη ἀναγνῶναι.

verses.english: And he said to them, "Surely you will say this parable to me: 'Physician, heal yourself! Whatever we heard happened at Capernaum, do here too, in your fatherland.'"
verses.greek: καὶ εἶπεν πρὸς αὐτούς· Πάντως ἐρεῖτέ μοι τὴν παραβολὴν ταύτην· Ἰατρέ, θεράπευσον σεαυτόν· ὅσα ἠκούσαμεν γενόμενα εἰς τὴν Καφαρναοὺμ ποίησον καὶ ὧδε ἐν τῇ πατρίδι σου.

verses.english: And he said, "Amen, I tell you: no prophet is acceptable in his fatherland."
verses.greek: εἶπεν δέ· Ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν ὅτι οὐδεὶς προφήτης δεκτός ἐστιν ἐν τῇ πατρίδι αὐτοῦ.

verses.english: And all in the assembly were filled with rage as they heard these things,
verses.greek: καὶ ἐπλήσθησαν πάντες θυμοῦ ἐν τῇ συναγωγῇ ἀκούοντες ταῦτα,

verses.english: and rising up they threw him out, outside the city, and led him to the brow of the mountain on which their city had been built, so as to throw him down the cliff.
verses.greek: καὶ ἀναστάντες ἐξέβαλον αὐτὸν ἔξω τῆς πόλεως, καὶ ἤγαγον αὐτὸν ἕως ὀφρύος τοῦ ὄρους ἐφ’ οὗ ἡ πόλις ᾠκοδόμητο αὐτῶν, ὥστε κατακρημνίσαι αὐτόν·

verses.english: But he, passing through the middle of them, went on his way.
verses.greek: αὐτὸς δὲ διελθὼν διὰ μέσου αὐτῶν ἐπορεύετο.

verses.english: As the sun was setting, all who had people sick with various diseases brought them to him; and he, laying his hands on each one of them, was healing them.
verses.greek: Δύνοντος δὲ τοῦ ἡλίου ἅπαντες ὅσοι εἶχον ἀσθενοῦντας νόσοις ποικίλαις ἤγαγον αὐτοὺς πρὸς αὐτόν· ὁ δὲ ἑνὶ ἑκάστῳ αὐτῶν τὰς χεῖρας ἐπιτιθεὶς ἐθεράπευεν αὐτούς.

verses.english: And daimons too were going out from many, crying out and saying, "You are the son of God!" And rebuking them, he would not let them speak, because they knew him to be the Anointed One.
verses.greek: ἐξήρχετο δὲ καὶ δαιμόνια ἀπὸ πολλῶν κραυγάζοντα καὶ λέγοντα ὅτι Σὺ εἶ ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ. καὶ ἐπιτιμῶν οὐκ εἴα αὐτὰ λαλεῖν, ὅτι ᾔδεισαν τὸν χριστὸν αὐτὸν εἶναι.

verses.english: When day came, going out, he journeyed to a desert place; and the crowds were searching for him, and they came up to him and were holding him back from journeying away from them.
verses.greek: Γενομένης δὲ ἡμέρας ἐξελθὼν ἐπορεύθη εἰς ἔρημον τόπον· καὶ οἱ ὄχλοι ἐπεζήτουν αὐτόν, καὶ ἦλθον ἕως αὐτοῦ, καὶ κατεῖχον αὐτὸν τοῦ μὴ πορεύεσθαι ἀπ’ αὐτῶν.

verses.english: But he said to them, "To the other cities also I must announce the good news of the kingdom of God, because for this I was sent."
verses.greek: ὁ δὲ εἶπεν πρὸς αὐτοὺς ὅτι Καὶ ταῖς ἑτέραις πόλεσιν εὐαγγελίσασθαί με δεῖ τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ θεοῦ, ὅτι ἐπὶ τοῦτο ἀπεστάλην.

verses.english: And he was proclaiming in the assemblies of Judea.
verses.greek: καὶ ἦν κηρύσσων εἰς τὰς συναγωγὰς τῆς Ἰουδαίας.

notes.explanation: Epiphanius, Pan. 42.11.4–5 (Holl 107–108): the text began »ἐν τῷ πεντεκαιδεκάτῳ ἔτει Τιβερίου Καίσαρος« and lacked Luke 1:1–2:52, the baptism (3:21–22) and the genealogy (3:23–38). Tertullian, Marc. 4.7.1: "Anno quintodecimo principatus Tiberiani proponit eum descendisse in civitatem Galilaeae Capharnaum." Irenaeus, Haer. 1.27.2 also opens Marcion's account with Jesus coming "in the times of Pontius Pilate". The witnesses join the date to the descent, so 3:2–4:15 is not printed (3:2–20 John's preaching; 4:1–13 temptation; 4:14–15 return to Galilee). Roth (2015) classes 3:2–20 and 4:14–15 as unattested rather than absent; the junction is the evidence for absence. The δέ of canonical 3:1 and the Καί of 4:31 are canonical Luke's connectives and are not printed (editorial junction; neither witness has them). The clauses naming Herod, Philip and Lysanias are not cited by any witness; they are printed in the NA27 wording within the attested verse.

Interpretation. In the Greek the verb has its ordinary geographical sense: from the hill country down to Capernaum on the lake. Tertullian reports that Marcion read it as a descent from heaven ("utique de caelo", Marc. 4.7.1). That is the reception of the text in Marcion's church, not a feature of its wording. Earlier versions of this note presented the heavenly descent as the meaning of the text; it is withdrawn.

Tertullian works through Marcion's text in order: the Capernaum exorcism in Marc. 4.7 (4:31–35), then Nazareth in 4.8.2–3 (4:16, 23, 29–30), then the evening healings and departure in 4.8.4–10 (4:40–43). This edition follows that order. Within it 4:23 ("whatever we heard happened at Capernaum") refers back to events already told. In canonical Luke the Nazareth scene comes first and 4:23 refers to deeds the reader has not yet seen. The order is attested; which direction the change went is not stated here (METHOD §10).

Tertullian, Marc. 4.7.9: "Exclamat ibidem spiritus daemonis, Quid nobis et tibi est Iesu? venisti perdere nos: scio qui sis, sanctus dei"; 4.7.13: "increpuit illum Iesus". The paraphrase attests 4:33, which Roth lists as unattested. Tertullian's quotation of 4:34 lacks Ἔα and Ναζαρηνέ. This is one witness, and a Latin quotation can drop an interjection and a title; Roth rates the absence of Ναζαρηνέ only "may not have been present". The NA27 wording is printed. Tertullian begins the next section with the name "Nazaraeus" (4.8.1). The previous text deleted Ναζαρηνέ; that went beyond the evidence and is reversed.

4:36–37 are printed in grey: no witness cites them, but they close the attested exorcism. 4:38–39 (Simon's mother-in-law) forms its own paragraph and no witness cites it; Tertullian passes from 4:35 (4.7.13) to Nazareth (4.8.2) and returns at 4:40 (4.8.4). A whole unattested pericope is not printed (METHOD §4.3).

notes.term: The Nazareth visit: what is attested
notes.explanation: Tertullian, Marc. 4.8.2–3: at Nazareth Jesus "is noted as having preached nothing new" and was thrown out "on account of a single proverb"; hands were laid on him, he was held, seized and dragged to the precipice, and he escaped "through their midst". This attests 4:16 (the visit and his preaching), a proverb (4:23, or 4:24), 4:29 and 4:30. 4:24 and 4:28 are not cited and are printed in grey.

notes.term: Absent from the Nazareth visit: 4:17–22 and 4:25–26
notes.explanation: 4:17–21 (the reading of Isaiah 61 and "today this scripture is fulfilled"): Tertullian's case in Marc. IV is that Jesus fulfils the Creator's prophets. A fulfilment of Isaiah announced in the synagogue would have been his best proof, and he says instead that Jesus preached "nothing new" there. 4:22 ("Is not this Joseph's son?"): Tertullian argues (4.7.7) that no one knew Jesus' tribe, people or house; the question would have served him and is not cited. 4:25–26 (Elijah and the widow of Sarepta): Tertullian names one proverb as the cause of the ejection, whereas in canonical Luke the Elijah and Elisha sayings provoke it. All three are classed "unattested, probably absent" (METHOD §3). 4:27 (Naaman) is attested, but inside the healing of the ten lepers (Epiphanius, sch. 48; Tertullian, Marc. 4.35.6); it is printed there. The previous text printed 4:22a; it is removed. The previous note headed "Excision of Biological Paternity" stated a motive for a change; the witnesses show only that the verse is absent.

Tertullian, Marc. 4.8.5: the spirits came out "vociferantes, Tu es filius dei" and were ordered to be silent. NA27 cites Marcion (McionT) with ℵ B C D L W and others against the addition of ὁ χριστός ("you are the Christ, the son of God") in A Q Θ Ψ and the Byzantine text. The closing clause "because they knew him to be the Anointed One" is not cited by Tertullian; it is printed in the NA27 wording within the attested verse.

Tertullian, Marc. 4.8.9: "In solitudinem procedit… Detentus a turbis, Oportet me, inquit, et aliis civitatibus annuntiare regnum dei." 4:44 is not cited and is printed in grey; NA27 reads "Judea" (ℵ B C L and others), against "Galilee" in A D Θ Ψ and the Byzantine text.

Interpretation, drawn from the attested text only. Jesus is introduced without ancestry, birth, prophetic announcement, baptism or testing. His first acts are teaching in a synagogue on the sabbath and an exorcism, and his hearers are said not to know where he comes from. The text gives no Davidic descent and no family claim. The library's thesis that the earliest gospel belongs to the Jerusalem community around James (Carriers of Living Water §1–3) is not contradicted by this: the setting is wholly Jewish (synagogue, sabbath, the kingdom of God). But the text in this section gives no support to a dynastic framing either. The reading of κατῆλθεν as a descent from heaven belongs to Marcion's church, not to the wording.
the emperor's "rule" and Pilate's "governing" are the same Greek word (ἡγεμών, one who leads). The English keeps the pair visible.
a tetrarch is literally "ruler of a fourth", a client ruler under Rome. The verb comes three times.

notes.term: The sentence has no main verb
notes.explanation: the date runs straight into "he came down" (4:31). The final comma is the Greek's.
the subject is not named until 4:35. Nothing in the Greek says where from.
plural in the Greek. It can mean "on the sabbath day", but the plural is kept.
the imperfect, "they kept being astounded". The verb means overwhelmed or struck out of one's composure.
the Greek word means a gathering, both the people gathered and the place. "Synagogue" is the word left untranslated.
in Greek a spirit-power, a lesser divine being. "Demon" brings in the later idea of a fallen angel. "A spirit of an unclean daimon" translates πνεῦμα δαιμονίου ἀκαθάρτου word for word.
a human being. The word does not say male. ἀνήρ is the word for a man.
a cry of displeasure or surprise. It can also be read as the imperative of ἐάω, "let alone!"

notes.term: τί ἡμῖν καὶ σοί, "what is there between us and you"
notes.explanation: a Hebrew idiom, literally "what to us and to you?" It means "we have nothing in common".
plural, although one daimon speaks.
an adjective, "the one from Nazara". Other derivations have been proposed (Hebrew nazir, "consecrated"; netser, "shoot"). The translation keeps the Greek word.

notes.term: ὁ ἅγιος τοῦ θεοῦ, "the holy one of God"
notes.explanation: lower case. The Greek is a description, not a title set apart by capitals.
to censure, to order sharply. The same verb is used for the daimons (4:41).
the verb is used for muzzling an animal. Here it means a harsh "be silent!"

notes.term: ἔξελθε ἀπ' αὐτοῦ, "go out from him"
notes.explanation: the same command Simon speaks about himself at 5:8 ("go out from me"). The English keeps them alike.
the same phrase returns at 5:19 and 6:8.
a different word from ἐξεπλήσσοντο (4:32) and from ἔκστασις (5:26).
the same word as in 4:32. Like the Hebrew davar, it can also mean "matter, thing": "what is this thing?"
a command from one set above.
a noise or echo. It is not the usual word for a report (φήμη).
the form of the name in this text, as in NA27 here.

notes.term: οὗ ἦν τεθραμμένος, "where he had been brought up"
notes.explanation: the verb τρέφω means to feed, nourish, rear.

notes.term: τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῶν σαββάτων, "the day of the sabbaths"
notes.explanation: plural, as at 4:31.
ἀνίστημι, to stand up, rise. The same verb is used at 4:29 ("rising up").
here a proverb. Luke uses the one word for both a proverb and a story. The English keeps the one word so the reader can see this.
one's native place, the land of one's fathers. "Home town" is correct in sense but loses the link with "father".
a Hebrew word ("firmly, truly") that the Greek leaves untranslated, so it is left untranslated here.
welcome. It is the word used for a sacrifice that is accepted.
hot passion, anger that flares up.
ἐκβάλλω, the verb also used for driving out daimons. The Greek says "threw him out outside the city".
the word covers both hill and mountain. "Mountain" is kept because the same word is used for the mountain of prayer (6:12) and the mountain of 9:28.
πόλις is kept as "city" throughout, as distinct from κώμη, "village".
to hurl down a precipice.

notes.term: διὰ μέσου αὐτῶν, "through the middle of them"
notes.explanation: cf. "into the middle" at 4:35.
literally "without strength, weak".
the imperfect, one after another. θεραπεύω (heal, tend) is kept apart from ἰάομαι (cure, 5:17).

notes.term: ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ, "the son of God"
notes.explanation: lower case. In Jewish usage it was a title of the king (Ps 2:7) and of the just. A capital "Son" in English assumes a later doctrine the Greek does not mark.
χριστός means anointed, the Greek for Hebrew mashiach. "Christ" makes it a name.
an uninhabited place, not necessarily sand.
the imperfect can mean "tried to hold him back". Both readings are open.
the same verb as "went on his way" (4:30). It returns throughout the text for the road.
a verb, not "preach the gospel".
necessity.
first the rule of a king, then the realm he rules. Read "reign" in "kingdom" as much as "realm".
the verb behind ἀπόστολος, "emissary" (6:13).
here probably the land of the Judeans as a whole, not only the southern district. The Greek name is kept.

chapters.title: Proto-Luke Chapter 2
chapters.preamble: Five scenes from Galilee: the call of the fishermen, the cleansing of a leper, the healing of a paralysed man, the call of a tax collector with the question about fasting, and two sabbath disputes. Tertullian works through all of them in order (Marc. 4.9–4.12) and Epiphanius quotes from three. The section is set inside Jewish practice. The cleansed leper is sent to the priest with the offering Moses commanded; in this text the reason given is "so that this may be a testimony to you". The sabbath disputes argue from what David did and from what the law permits. The witnesses also show the Marcionite church explaining some of this away: Tertullian reports that Marcion read the leper's offering as a concession to the man's habit. A community does not insert into its own scripture a passage it has to explain away, so these passages are older than the Marcionite reading of them (interpretation).

verses.english: And it happened, while the crowd was pressing on him and hearing the word of God, that he was standing beside the lake of Gennesaret,
verses.greek: Ἐγένετο δὲ ἐν τῷ τὸν ὄχλον ἐπικεῖσθαι αὐτῷ καὶ ἀκούειν τὸν λόγον τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ αὐτὸς ἦν ἑστὼς παρὰ τὴν λίμνην Γεννησαρέτ,

verses.english: and he saw two boats standing beside the lake; but the fishermen had stepped out of them and were washing the nets.
verses.greek: καὶ εἶδεν δύο πλοῖα ἑστῶτα παρὰ τὴν λίμνην, οἱ δὲ ἁλιεῖς ἀπ’ αὐτῶν ἀποβάντες ἔπλυνον τὰ δίκτυα.

verses.english: Getting into one of the boats, which was Simon's, he asked him to put out a little from the land; and sitting down, he was teaching the crowds from the boat.
verses.greek: ἐμβὰς δὲ εἰς ἓν τῶν πλοίων, ὃ ἦν Σίμωνος, ἠρώτησεν αὐτὸν ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς ἐπαναγαγεῖν ὀλίγον, καθίσας δὲ ἐκ τοῦ πλοίου ἐδίδασκεν τοὺς ὄχλους.

verses.english: When he stopped speaking, he said to Simon, "Put out into the deep, and let down your nets for a catch."
verses.greek: ὡς δὲ ἐπαύσατο λαλῶν, εἶπεν πρὸς τὸν Σίμωνα· Ἐπανάγαγε εἰς τὸ βάθος καὶ χαλάσατε τὰ δίκτυα ὑμῶν εἰς ἄγραν.

verses.english: And Simon answered and said, "Overseer, through the whole night we toiled and took nothing; but at your word I will let down the nets."
verses.greek: καὶ ἀποκριθεὶς Σίμων εἶπεν· Ἐπιστάτα, δι’ ὅλης νυκτὸς κοπιάσαντες οὐδὲν ἐλάβομεν, ἐπὶ δὲ τῷ ῥήματί σου χαλάσω τὰ δίκτυα.

verses.english: And doing this, they enclosed a great multitude of fish, and their nets were tearing.
verses.greek: καὶ τοῦτο ποιήσαντες συνέκλεισαν πλῆθος ἰχθύων πολύ, διερρήσσετο δὲ τὰ δίκτυα αὐτῶν.

verses.english: And they signalled to their partners in the other boat to come and help them; and they came and filled both boats, so that they were sinking.
verses.greek: καὶ κατένευσαν τοῖς μετόχοις ἐν τῷ ἑτέρῳ πλοίῳ τοῦ ἐλθόντας συλλαβέσθαι αὐτοῖς· καὶ ἦλθον, καὶ ἔπλησαν ἀμφότερα τὰ πλοῖα ὥστε βυθίζεσθαι αὐτά.

verses.english: Seeing it, Simon Peter fell at the knees of Jesus, saying, "Go out from me, because I am a sinful man, lord."
verses.greek: ἰδὼν δὲ Σίμων Πέτρος προσέπεσεν τοῖς γόνασιν Ἰησοῦ λέγων· Ἔξελθε ἀπ’ ἐμοῦ, ὅτι ἀνὴρ ἁμαρτωλός εἰμι, κύριε·

verses.english: For astonishment had seized him and all those with him at the catch of the fish which they had taken,
verses.greek: θάμβος γὰρ περιέσχεν αὐτὸν καὶ πάντας τοὺς σὺν αὐτῷ ἐπὶ τῇ ἄγρᾳ τῶν ἰχθύων ὧν συνέλαβον,

verses.english: and likewise also Jacob and John, sons of Zebedee, who were sharers with Simon. And Jesus said to Simon, "Do not be afraid; from now on you will be catching humans alive."
verses.greek: ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ Ἰάκωβον καὶ Ἰωάννην υἱοὺς Ζεβεδαίου, οἳ ἦσαν κοινωνοὶ τῷ Σίμωνι. καὶ εἶπεν πρὸς τὸν Σίμωνα ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Μὴ φοβοῦ· ἀπὸ τοῦ νῦν ἀνθρώπους ἔσῃ ζωγρῶν.

verses.english: And having brought the boats down onto the land, letting go of everything, they followed him.
verses.greek: καὶ καταγαγόντες τὰ πλοῖα ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν ἀφέντες πάντα ἠκολούθησαν αὐτῷ.

verses.english: And it happened while he was in one of the cities, that look, a man full of leprosy; and seeing Jesus, falling on his face, he begged him, saying, "Lord, if you want, you are able to cleanse me."
verses.greek: Καὶ ἐγένετο ἐν τῷ εἶναι αὐτὸν ἐν μιᾷ τῶν πόλεων καὶ ἰδοὺ ἀνὴρ πλήρης λέπρας· ἰδὼν δὲ τὸν Ἰησοῦν πεσὼν ἐπὶ πρόσωπον ἐδεήθη αὐτοῦ λέγων· Κύριε, ἐὰν θέλῃς δύνασαί με καθαρίσαι.

verses.english: And stretching out his hand he touched him, saying, "I want it: be cleansed." And at once the leprosy went away from him.
verses.greek: καὶ ἐκτείνας τὴν χεῖρα ἥψατο αὐτοῦ λέγων· Θέλω, καθαρίσθητι· καὶ εὐθέως ἡ λέπρα ἀπῆλθεν ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ.

verses.english: And he ordered him to tell no one: "But go away, show yourself to the priest, and bring an offering for your cleansing, just as Moses commanded, so that this may be a testimony to you."
verses.greek: καὶ αὐτὸς παρήγγειλεν αὐτῷ μηδενὶ εἰπεῖν, ἀλλὰ ἀπελθὼν δεῖξον σεαυτὸν τῷ ἱερεῖ, καὶ προσένεγκε περὶ τοῦ καθαρισμοῦ σου καθὼς προσέταξεν Μωϋσῆς, ἵνα ᾖ μαρτύριον τοῦτο ὑμῖν.

verses.english: But the word about him was spreading all the more, and many crowds were coming together to hear and to be healed of their weaknesses;
verses.greek: διήρχετο δὲ μᾶλλον ὁ λόγος περὶ αὐτοῦ, καὶ συνήρχοντο ὄχλοι πολλοὶ ἀκούειν καὶ θεραπεύεσθαι ἀπὸ τῶν ἀσθενειῶν αὐτῶν·

verses.english: but he himself was withdrawing in the deserts and praying.
verses.greek: αὐτὸς δὲ ἦν ὑποχωρῶν ἐν ταῖς ἐρήμοις καὶ προσευχόμενος.

verses.english: And it happened on one of the days, as he was teaching, that Pharisees and teachers of the law were sitting there, who had come out of every village of Galilee and Judea and from Jerusalem; and power of the Lord was there for him to cure.
verses.greek: Καὶ ἐγένετο ἐν μιᾷ τῶν ἡμερῶν καὶ αὐτὸς ἦν διδάσκων, καὶ ἦσαν καθήμενοι Φαρισαῖοι καὶ νομοδιδάσκαλοι οἳ ἦσαν ἐληλυθότες ἐκ πάσης κώμης τῆς Γαλιλαίας καὶ Ἰουδαίας καὶ Ἰερουσαλήμ· καὶ δύναμις κυρίου ἦν εἰς τὸ ἰᾶσθαι αὐτόν.

verses.english: And look, men carrying on a bed a person who had been paralysed, and they were seeking to bring him in and lay him before him.
verses.greek: καὶ ἰδοὺ ἄνδρες φέροντες ἐπὶ κλίνης ἄνθρωπον ὃς ἦν παραλελυμένος, καὶ ἐζήτουν αὐτὸν εἰσενεγκεῖν καὶ θεῖναι αὐτὸν ἐνώπιον αὐτοῦ.

verses.english: And not finding by what way they might bring him in because of the crowd, going up onto the roof they let him down through the tiles with the little bed into the middle, in front of Jesus.
verses.greek: καὶ μὴ εὑρόντες ποίας εἰσενέγκωσιν αὐτὸν διὰ τὸν ὄχλον ἀναβάντες ἐπὶ τὸ δῶμα διὰ τῶν κεράμων καθῆκαν αὐτὸν σὺν τῷ κλινιδίῳ εἰς τὸ μέσον ἔμπροσθεν τοῦ Ἰησοῦ.

verses.english: And seeing their trust he said, "Human, your sins have been let go for you."
verses.greek: καὶ ἰδὼν τὴν πίστιν αὐτῶν εἶπεν· Ἄνθρωπε, ἀφέωνταί σοι αἱ ἁμαρτίαι σου.

verses.english: And the scribes and the Pharisees began to reason, saying, "Who is this who speaks blasphemies? Who is able to let sins go except God alone?"
verses.greek: καὶ ἤρξαντο διαλογίζεσθαι οἱ γραμματεῖς καὶ οἱ Φαρισαῖοι λέγοντες· Τίς ἐστιν οὗτος ὃς λαλεῖ βλασφημίας; τίς δύναται ἁμαρτίας ἀφεῖναι εἰ μὴ μόνος ὁ θεός;

verses.english: But Jesus, recognising their reasonings, answered and said to them, "Why are you reasoning in your hearts?
verses.greek: ἐπιγνοὺς δὲ ὁ Ἰησοῦς τοὺς διαλογισμοὺς αὐτῶν ἀποκριθεὶς εἶπεν πρὸς αὐτούς· Τί διαλογίζεσθε ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις ὑμῶν;

verses.english: Which is easier: to say, 'Your sins have been let go for you,' or to say, 'Get up and walk about'?
verses.greek: τί ἐστιν εὐκοπώτερον, εἰπεῖν· Ἀφέωνταί σοι αἱ ἁμαρτίαι σου, ἢ εἰπεῖν· Ἔγειρε καὶ περιπάτει;

verses.english: But so that you may know that the son of the human has authority on the earth to let sins go"—he said to the paralysed man—"I say to you, get up, and take up your mattress, and journey to your house."
verses.greek: ἵνα δὲ εἰδῆτε ὅτι ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἐξουσίαν ἔχει ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς ἀφιέναι ἁμαρτίας— εἶπεν τῷ παραλελυμένῳ· Σοὶ λέγω, ἔγειρε καὶ ἆρον τὸν κράβαττόν σου καὶ πορεύου εἰς τὸν οἶκόν σου.

verses.english: And at once standing up before them, taking up what he had been lying on, he went away to his house, giving glory to God.
verses.greek: καὶ παραχρῆμα ἀναστὰς ἐνώπιον αὐτῶν, ἄρας ἐφ’ ὃ κατέκειτο, ἀπῆλθεν εἰς τὸν οἶκον αὐτοῦ δοξάζων τὸν θεόν.

verses.english: And amazement took hold of all, and they were giving glory to God, and they were filled with fear, saying, "We have seen things against all expectation today."
verses.greek: καὶ ἔκστασις ἔλαβεν ἅπαντας καὶ ἐδόξαζον τὸν θεόν, καὶ ἐπλήσθησαν φόβου λέγοντες ὅτι Εἴδομεν παράδοξα σήμερον.

verses.english: And after these things he went out and observed a tax collector by name Levi sitting at the tax office, and he said to him, "Follow me."
verses.greek: Καὶ μετὰ ταῦτα ἐξῆλθεν καὶ ἐθεάσατο τελώνην ὀνόματι Λευὶν καθήμενον ἐπὶ τὸ τελώνιον, καὶ εἶπεν αὐτῷ· Ἀκολούθει μοι.

verses.english: And leaving everything behind, standing up, he was following him.
verses.greek: καὶ καταλιπὼν πάντα ἀναστὰς ἠκολούθει αὐτῷ.

verses.english: And Levi made a great reception for him in his house; and there was a large crowd of tax collectors and of others who were reclining at table with them.
verses.greek: Καὶ ἐποίησεν δοχὴν μεγάλην Λευὶς αὐτῷ ἐν τῇ οἰκίᾳ αὐτοῦ· καὶ ἦν ὄχλος πολὺς τελωνῶν καὶ ἄλλων οἳ ἦσαν μετ’ αὐτῶν κατακείμενοι.

verses.english: And the Pharisees and their scribes were grumbling to his learners, saying, "Why do you eat and drink with the tax collectors and sinners?"
verses.greek: καὶ ἐγόγγυζον οἱ Φαρισαῖοι καὶ οἱ γραμματεῖς αὐτῶν πρὸς τοὺς μαθητὰς αὐτοῦ λέγοντες· Διὰ τί μετὰ τῶν τελωνῶν καὶ ἁμαρτωλῶν ἐσθίετε καὶ πίνετε;

verses.english: And answering, Jesus said to them, "Those who are healthy have no need of a physician, but those who are in a bad way.
verses.greek: καὶ ἀποκριθεὶς ὁ Ἰησοῦς εἶπεν πρὸς αὐτούς· Οὐ χρείαν ἔχουσιν οἱ ὑγιαίνοντες ἰατροῦ ἀλλὰ οἱ κακῶς ἔχοντες·

verses.english: I have not come to call just people, but sinners to a change of mind."
verses.greek: οὐκ ἐλήλυθα καλέσαι δικαίους ἀλλὰ ἁμαρτωλοὺς εἰς μετάνοιαν.

verses.english: But they said to him, "The learners of John fast often and make petitions, likewise also those of the Pharisees; but yours eat and drink."
verses.greek: Οἱ δὲ εἶπαν πρὸς αὐτόν· Οἱ μαθηταὶ Ἰωάννου νηστεύουσιν πυκνὰ καὶ δεήσεις ποιοῦνται, ὁμοίως καὶ οἱ τῶν Φαρισαίων, οἱ δὲ σοὶ ἐσθίουσιν καὶ πίνουσιν.

verses.english: But Jesus said to them, "You cannot make the sons of the bridal chamber fast while the bridegroom is with them, can you?
verses.greek: ὁ δὲ Ἰησοῦς εἶπεν πρὸς αὐτούς· Μὴ δύνασθε τοὺς υἱοὺς τοῦ νυμφῶνος ἐν ᾧ ὁ νυμφίος μετ’ αὐτῶν ἐστιν ποιῆσαι νηστεῦσαι;

verses.english: But days will come, and when the bridegroom is taken away from them, then they will fast in those days."
verses.greek: ἐλεύσονται δὲ ἡμέραι, καὶ ὅταν ἀπαρθῇ ἀπ’ αὐτῶν ὁ νυμφίος τότε νηστεύσουσιν ἐν ἐκείναις ταῖς ἡμέραις.

verses.english: And he was also saying a parable to them: "No one, tearing a patch from a new garment, puts it on an old garment; otherwise he will both tear the new, and the patch from the new will not agree with the old.
verses.greek: ἔλεγεν δὲ καὶ παραβολὴν πρὸς αὐτοὺς ὅτι Οὐδεὶς ἐπίβλημα ἀπὸ ἱματίου καινοῦ σχίσας ἐπιβάλλει ἐπὶ ἱμάτιον παλαιόν· εἰ δὲ μή γε, καὶ τὸ καινὸν σχίσει καὶ τῷ παλαιῷ οὐ συμφωνήσει τὸ ἐπίβλημα τὸ ἀπὸ τοῦ καινοῦ.

verses.english: And no one puts young wine into old wineskins; otherwise the young wine will burst the skins, and it will be poured out, and the skins will be destroyed.
verses.greek: καὶ οὐδεὶς βάλλει οἶνον νέον εἰς ἀσκοὺς παλαιούς· εἰ δὲ μή γε, ῥήξει ὁ οἶνος ὁ νέος τοὺς ἀσκούς, καὶ αὐτὸς ἐκχυθήσεται καὶ οἱ ἀσκοὶ ἀπολοῦνται·

verses.english: But young wine must be put into new wineskins."
verses.greek: ἀλλὰ οἶνον νέον εἰς ἀσκοὺς καινοὺς βλητέον.

verses.english: And it happened on a sabbath that he was going through grainfields, and his learners were plucking and eating the heads of grain, rubbing them with their hands.
verses.greek: Ἐγένετο δὲ ἐν σαββάτῳ διαπορεύεσθαι αὐτὸν διὰ σπορίμων, καὶ ἔτιλλον οἱ μαθηταὶ αὐτοῦ καὶ ἤσθιον τοὺς στάχυας ψώχοντες ταῖς χερσίν.

verses.english: But some of the Pharisees said, "Why are you doing what is not permitted on the sabbaths?"
verses.greek: τινὲς δὲ τῶν Φαρισαίων εἶπαν· Τί ποιεῖτε ὃ οὐκ ἔξεστιν τοῖς σάββασιν;

verses.english: And answering them, Jesus said, "Have you not even read this, what David did when he was hungry, he and those who were with him,
verses.greek: καὶ ἀποκριθεὶς πρὸς αὐτοὺς εἶπεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Οὐδὲ τοῦτο ἀνέγνωτε ὃ ἐποίησεν Δαυὶδ ὅτε ἐπείνασεν αὐτὸς καὶ οἱ μετ’ αὐτοῦ ὄντες;

verses.english: how he went into the house of God and, taking the loaves of the setting-forth, he ate and gave to those with him, which it is not permitted to eat except for the priests alone?"
verses.greek: ὡς εἰσῆλθεν εἰς τὸν οἶκον τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ τοὺς ἄρτους τῆς προθέσεως λαβὼν ἔφαγεν καὶ ἔδωκεν τοῖς μετ’ αὐτοῦ, οὓς οὐκ ἔξεστιν φαγεῖν εἰ μὴ μόνους τοὺς ἱερεῖς;

verses.english: And he was saying to them, "The son of the human is lord also of the sabbath."
verses.greek: καὶ ἔλεγεν αὐτοῖς· Κύριός ἐστιν ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου καὶ τοῦ σαββάτου.

verses.english: And it happened on another sabbath that he went into the assembly and was teaching; and there was a person there, and his right hand was dry.
verses.greek: Ἐγένετο δὲ ἐν ἑτέρῳ σαββάτῳ εἰσελθεῖν αὐτὸν εἰς τὴν συναγωγὴν καὶ διδάσκειν· καὶ ἦν ἄνθρωπος ἐκεῖ καὶ ἡ χεὶρ αὐτοῦ ἡ δεξιὰ ἦν ξηρά·

verses.english: And the scribes and the Pharisees were watching him closely, whether he heals on the sabbath, so that they might find how to accuse him.
verses.greek: παρετηροῦντο δὲ οἱ γραμματεῖς καὶ οἱ Φαρισαῖοι εἰ ἐν τῷ σαββάτῳ θεραπεύει, ἵνα εὕρωσιν κατηγορεῖν αὐτοῦ.

verses.english: But he knew their reasonings, and he said to the man who had the dry hand, "Get up and stand into the middle." And standing up, he stood.
verses.greek: αὐτὸς δὲ ᾔδει τοὺς διαλογισμοὺς αὐτῶν, εἶπεν δὲ τῷ ἀνδρὶ τῷ ξηρὰν ἔχοντι τὴν χεῖρα· Ἔγειρε καὶ στῆθι εἰς τὸ μέσον· καὶ ἀναστὰς ἔστη.

verses.english: And Jesus said to them, "I ask you if it is permitted on the sabbath to do good or to do evil, to save a soul or to destroy it?"
verses.greek: εἶπεν δὲ ὁ Ἰησοῦς πρὸς αὐτούς· Ἐπερωτῶ ὑμᾶς, εἰ ἔξεστιν τῷ σαββάτῳ ἀγαθοποιῆσαι ἢ κακοποιῆσαι, ψυχὴν σῶσαι ἢ ἀπολέσαι;

verses.english: And looking around at them all, he said to him, "Stretch out your hand." And he did, and his hand was restored.
verses.greek: καὶ περιβλεψάμενος πάντας αὐτοὺς εἶπεν αὐτῷ· Ἔκτεινον τὴν χεῖρά σου· ὁ δὲ ἐποίησεν, καὶ ἀπεκατεστάθη ἡ χεὶρ αὐτοῦ.

verses.english: But they were filled with mindlessness, and were discussing with one another what they might do to Jesus.
verses.greek: αὐτοὶ δὲ ἐπλήσθησαν ἀνοίας, καὶ διελάλουν πρὸς ἀλλήλους τί ἂν ποιήσαιεν τῷ Ἰησοῦ.

notes.explanation: Tertullian, Marc. 4.9.1–2: Jesus took Simon and the sons of Zebedee from fishing, "saying to Peter, who was afraid at the abundant catch of fish, Do not fear, for from now on you will be catching men"; "they left their boats and followed him". This attests 5:2, 5:9–11 and the catch itself. 5:1 and 5:3–8 are not cited and are printed in grey. One library document (No Original Exists, App. B) lists ἐπιστάτα at 5:5 as a Marcionite reading; no witness cites 5:5, so the claim is not supported and is listed for correction.

Tertullian, Marc. 4.9.3–10, and Epiphanius, sch. 1 with refutation 1. NA27 reads ἰδὼν δέ at 5:12 and λέγων at 5:13 (SBLGNT: καὶ ἰδών, εἰπών); checked on the NA27 page. At 5:14 Epiphanius quotes the ending as »ἵνα ᾖ μαρτύριον τοῦτο ὑμῖν« and contrasts it with the canonical »εἰς μαρτύριον αὐτοῖς«; Tertullian has "Ut sit vobis in testimonium" (4.9.10). Two witnesses agree on the purpose clause and the second person; the Greek of Epiphanius is printed. D and the Old Latin read ἵνα εἰς μαρτύριον ᾖ ὑμῖν τοῦτο, and NA27 cites Marcion there. Whether εἰς stood in the text (Tertullian's "in testimonium", D) is left open. Tertullian also has "offer the gift" (munus); one witness, not adopted.

notes.term: "So that this may be a testimony to you"
notes.explanation: Interpretation. Both witnesses attest that Jesus sends the man to the priest to make the offering Moses commanded. In canonical Luke the testimony is "to them" (the priests); in this text it is "for you" (the man and his community), and it rests on doing what the Torah prescribes. Tertullian records the Marcionite explanation: Jesus, being kind and knowing the man would keep the law anyway, allowed it (Marc. 4.9.10). That is reception (METHOD §7): the community that read this text had to explain away its Torah observance, so the passage was not written to fit that community's theology. The observance is consistent with the library's thesis of a Torah-keeping Jewish community behind the text (Carriers of Living Water §3.4).

Tertullian, Marc. 4.10.1–14, and Epiphanius, sch. 2. Tertullian cites the scribes' objection ("Who forgives sins but God alone?") and the command "Arise and take up your mat". The Latin of 4.10.1 as transcribed on tertullian.org breaks off after "tolle"; Evans' English translation of the same edition reads "Arise and take up thy bed", and NA27 cites Marcion for τὸν κράβαττον. The reading ἔγειρε καὶ ἆρον τὸν κράβαττόν σου καὶ πορεύου is printed: ἆρον and καί with ℵ D 1424; κράβαττον with D 1424 and the Old Latin c r1. This is a retroversion from Latin; grabatum is the Latin form of κράβαττος, not of κλινίδιον. Epiphanius quotes 5:24a in the order of Mark and Matthew; Roth marks the order uncertain, and NA27's order is kept. 5:18 includes NA27's bracketed [αὐτόν]. 5:19, 5:22–23 and 5:25 are not cited and are printed in grey.

notes.term: Levi and the question of fasting (5:27–38)
notes.explanation: Tertullian, Marc. 4.11.1–10: the tax collector chosen, the physician saying ("medicum sanis non esse necessarium sed male habentibus"), John's disciples who fast and pray, the bridegroom, and the patch and wineskins. 5:28–29 and 5:32 are not cited and are printed in grey. At 5:34 NA27 has ὁ Ἰησοῦς (SBLGNT omits it); Tertullian's "non possent ieiunare filii sponsi" agrees with ℵ* D it (δύνανται… νηστεύειν), which Roth rates possible, so it is noted, not printed. At 5:38 NA27 cites the Dialogue of Adamantius (McionA) for βάλλουσιν and "both are preserved"; Roth marks the attestation uncertain.

"No one after drinking old wine wants new, for he says, The old is good." No witness cites it. Tertullian spends Marc. 4.11.9–11 arguing that old and new come from one God, and the saying would have served that argument. It is classed "unattested, probably absent" and not printed. It is also absent from D and the Old Latin (NA27).

Tertullian, Marc. 4.12.1–14; Epiphanius, sch. 21 (6:3–4) and sch. 3 (6:5). NA27 reads ὅτε at 6:3 (SBLGNT ὁπότε) and brackets [ὄντες] (6:3) and [ὡς] (6:4); the bracketed words are printed, because Epiphanius' quotation skips the clause rather than reading it without them. At 6:5 Epiphanius quotes »κύριός ἐστιν ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου καὶ τοῦ σαββάτου«; this is the reading of A D L Θ Ψ and the Byzantine text, cited in NA27 for Marcion (McionE), and is printed. D places 6:5 after 6:10; Roth leaves the position open, and the canonical position is kept. At 6:9 NA27 cites Marcion for its own text (εἰ ἔξεστιν; ἀπολέσαι). 6:8 is cited only in a passage of Adamantius whose link to Marcion's text Roth marks uncertain; it is printed in grey with 6:10–11.

Interpretation. The disputes are argued from inside the law: the precedent of David from scripture, and the question what the law permits on the sabbath (to do good, to save life). Tertullian reads "lord of the sabbath" as proof that Jesus belonged to the Creator (4.12.11); that is his polemic. On the text alone the sabbath is not set aside; its proper use is argued, as in other Jewish debates of the period.

notes.term: Ἐγένετο δὲ… καί, "and it happened… that"
notes.explanation: a Hebrew way of opening a story (wayehi). Kept, because it marks the start of a new scene.
Luke calls it a lake. The other gospels call it a sea (θάλασσα).
the first verb is singular (to Simon), the second plural (to all in the boat). The English cannot show this; the Greek makes it plain.
the same root returns at 6:48, the house built "deep".
one set over others, a foreman or chief. Only Luke uses this word, and it differs from κύριε, "lord" (5:8), and from διδάσκαλε, "teacher". It is kept apart from both.
a thing said, an utterance. It is a different word from λόγος (5:1). English has only "word" for both.
the imperfect, beginning to tear.
two different words. μέτοχος is one who takes part; κοινωνός is one who holds something in common.

notes.term: Ἔξελθε ἀπ' ἐμοῦ, "go out from me"
notes.explanation: the words Jesus spoke to the daimon (4:35, "go out from him").
here the word for a male, not ἄνθρωπος.
the ordinary address to a superior, also "sir". It is in lower case because it is not the divine name.
a Greek name meaning "stone, rock" (cf. πέτρα, "rock", 6:48).
as in 4:36.
the Greek is the patriarch's name, Jacob. "James" comes from a later Latin form (Iacomus) of the same name and hides this.
the verb means to take alive. It is used of taking prisoners alive instead of killing them.
human beings, not men only.
ἀφίημι, the same verb used for sins "let go" at 5:20. "Left everything" is correct but hides that it is one verb.
a word that points, "see!" It is often left out in English. It is kept here.
in the Greek Bible it covers a range of skin diseases that made a person unclean, not only Hansen's disease.
the capital is only the start of the sentence. The address is "lord, sir", as at 5:8.
to make clean, in the sense of purity under the law, not only of health.
"if you want… I want". The plain verb of willing is repeated.

notes.term: μηδενὶ εἰπεῖν, ἀλλὰ ἀπελθὼν δεῖξον, "to tell no one
notes.explanation: but go away, show": the command moves from reported speech to direct speech. The Greek does this, and the English keeps it.

notes.term: ἵνα ᾖ μαρτύριον τοῦτο ὑμῖν, "so that this may be a testimony to you"
notes.explanation: the reading of this text, "this" and "to you" in the plural. Canonical Luke has "for a testimony to them".
here the talk or report about him.
the general word for illness, literally lack of strength.

notes.term: ἦν ὑποχωρῶν… καὶ προσευχόμενος, "was withdrawing… and praying"
notes.explanation: the imperfect, a habit ("he used to withdraw").
plural, uninhabited places.
κύριος without the article, in the way the Greek Bible renders the divine name. Here it means God, not Jesus, so it takes a capital.

notes.term: εἰς τὸ ἰᾶσθαι αὐτόν, "for him to cure"
notes.explanation: the Greek is ambiguous. It can mean that the power was there for him to cure with, or that it was there to cure him (the sick). The first is the usual reading.
kept apart from θεραπεύω, "heal" (4:40; 5:15).
three different words. κράβαττος, a poor man's pallet, is the reading of this text at 5:24; canonical Luke has κλινίδιον there.
a perfect passive, literally "loosened at the side".
as at 4:35.
confidence placed in a person. "Faith" now suggests holding a set of beliefs, which the word does not mean here. It is "their" trust, which includes the men who carried him.
a plain address to a person, neither warm nor cold.

the perfect passive of ἀφίημι, to let go, release, leave. The passive names no one who lets them go. "Forgiven" is a correct sense, but it hides that this is the verb of 5:11 ("letting go of everything") and of release in general.
the word means injurious, slanderous speech. Here it is speech that injures God.
to argue it through inside oneself. It is not the same as speaking aloud.
ἐγείρω, to rouse, raise, get up. It is kept apart from ἀνίστημι, "stand up" (5:25).

notes.term: ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου, "the son of the human"
notes.explanation: ἄνθρωπος is a human being, not a male. The Greek has the article twice ("the son of the human"). Behind it lies the Aramaic bar enasha, which can mean simply "a human being". "The son of man" is the traditional rendering. This rendering keeps the Greek word, without capitals.
the same word means land and earth.
the road verb (4:30, 4:42).

notes.term: δοξάζων τὸν θεόν, "giving glory to God"
notes.explanation: δοξάζω, to give glory, honour. δόξα is radiance and honour.
literally "standing outside oneself". In English "ecstasy" now means rapture, which is not the sense.
the word means fear. It is not softened to "awe".
literally "contrary to opinion, beyond what is thought".
a collector of tolls and customs, who leased the right to collect from the authorities.
καταλείπω, a different verb from ἀφίημι in 5:11.
the imperfect, he began to follow and went on following.
a banquet, from δέχομαι, "receive".
people lay on couches to eat at a formal meal.
a μαθητής is one who learns from a teacher. "Disciple" is the Latin word for the same thing, but it is now heard as a religious title.
a word that sounds like what it means, a low muttering.
in use, people who break the law, wrongdoers. Here it is also a social label for those outside observance. The etymology ("missing the mark") is not the meaning.

notes.term: οἱ κακῶς ἔχοντες, "those who are in a bad way"
notes.explanation: literally "those having it badly", the sick.
without the article, "just ones". δίκαιος means upright, in right relation to the law and to God. "Righteous" adds a churchly tone.

the Greek word says exactly that, a change of mind or of thinking. "Repentance" comes from the Latin paenitentia, which adds the idea of doing penance. In Jewish use the idea answers to the Hebrew shuv, "to turn back".
δέησις is a request made out of need. It is not the general word for prayer (προσευχή, 6:12).

notes.term: τοὺς υἱοὺς τοῦ νυμφῶνος, "the sons of the bridal chamber"
notes.explanation: a Semitic idiom for the bridegroom's attendants, the wedding guests. Kept word for word.
a question that expects the answer "no".
lifted off, removed.
two different words. καινός is new in kind, fresh, not worn. νέος is new in time, young. "Young wine" keeps the difference that "new wine" would hide.
be in harmony with, sound together.
ἀπόλλυμι, the verb of 4:34 ("destroy us").
spilled.
a verbal adjective of necessity.
literally "sown fields".
"it is not allowed". "Lawful" is correct, but it suggests a legal code more than the Greek word does.
plural, as at 4:31.

notes.term: τοὺς ἄρτους τῆς προθέσεως, "the loaves of the setting-forth"
notes.explanation: the bread laid out before God in the sanctuary. The Hebrew is lechem ha-panim, "bread of the face".
here "owner, master" of the sabbath. Lower case, because it is not the divine name. This text reads καί, "also", before "of the sabbath".
the word means dry, as in dry land. "Withered" is an interpretation of what was wrong with the hand.
to watch with hostile intent, to lie in wait.

notes.term: Ἔγειρε καὶ στῆθι εἰς τὸ μέσον, "get up and stand into the middle"
notes.explanation: εἰς with movement, "into". It is the same middle as 4:35 and 5:19.
the word for a male here.
ψυχή is the living self, the life a person has. "Save a life" gives the sense; "soul" keeps the word, which returns at 9:24 and 12:19–20. σῴζω is to save, rescue, make well.
ἀπόλλυμι, as at 4:34 and 5:37.
put back to its former state.
ἄνοια is the lack of understanding (νοῦς), folly. It can also be the frenzy of losing one's reason. "Fury" gives only the second sense.

chapters.title: Proto-Luke Chapter 3
chapters.preamble: The choosing of the twelve and the teaching given on the level place. Tertullian works through the sermon almost line by line (Marc. 4.13–4.17), so for this chapter the evidence is dense, and in several places the witnesses show the wording of Marcion's text where it differs from the canonical one. The beatitude is spoken of the destitute in the third person: "Fortunate are the destitute, because theirs is the kingdom of God." Tertullian notes that the Greek word means beggars. Beatitudes on the destitute, the hungry and those who weep are matched by woes on the rich, the full and those who laugh. Then come the love of enemies, compassion, not judging, the measure that is returned, the two trees and the two treasures, and the question "Why do you call me 'lord, lord', and do not do what I say?". The emphasis throughout falls on what a person does. Three of the sayings the library pairs with the Epistle of James (6:24, 6:37, 6:46) are attested by the witnesses.

verses.english: And it happened in these days that he went out into the mountain to pray, and he was spending the whole night in the prayer of God.
verses.greek: Ἐγένετο δὲ ἐν ταῖς ἡμέραις ταύταις ἐξελθεῖν αὐτὸν εἰς τὸ ὄρος προσεύξασθαι, καὶ ἦν διανυκτερεύων ἐν τῇ προσευχῇ τοῦ θεοῦ.

verses.english: And when it became day, he called his learners to him, and choosing twelve from them, whom he also named emissaries:
verses.greek: καὶ ὅτε ἐγένετο ἡμέρα, προσεφώνησεν τοὺς μαθητὰς αὐτοῦ, καὶ ἐκλεξάμενος ἀπ’ αὐτῶν δώδεκα, οὓς καὶ ἀποστόλους ὠνόμασεν,

verses.english: Simon, whom he also named Peter, and Andrew his brother, and Jacob and John, and Philip and Bartholomew,
verses.greek: Σίμωνα ὃν καὶ ὠνόμασεν Πέτρον καὶ Ἀνδρέαν τὸν ἀδελφὸν αὐτοῦ καὶ Ἰάκωβον καὶ Ἰωάννην καὶ Φίλιππον καὶ Βαρθολομαῖον

verses.english: and Matthew and Thomas, and Jacob son of Alphaeus, and Simon called the zealot,
verses.greek: καὶ Μαθθαῖον καὶ Θωμᾶν καὶ Ἰάκωβον Ἁλφαίου καὶ Σίμωνα τὸν καλούμενον ζηλωτὴν

verses.english: and Judas of Jacob, and Judas Iscarioth, who became a traitor.
verses.greek: καὶ Ἰούδαν Ἰακώβου καὶ Ἰούδαν Ἰσκαριὼθ ὃς ἐγένετο προδότης.

verses.english: And coming down with them, he stood on a level place, and a large crowd of his learners, and a great multitude of the people from all Judea and Jerusalem and the seacoast of Tyre and Sidon,
verses.greek: Καὶ καταβὰς μετ’ αὐτῶν ἔστη ἐπὶ τόπου πεδινοῦ, καὶ ὄχλος πολὺς μαθητῶν αὐτοῦ, καὶ πλῆθος πολὺ τοῦ λαοῦ ἀπὸ πάσης τῆς Ἰουδαίας καὶ Ἰερουσαλὴμ καὶ τῆς παραλίου Τύρου καὶ Σιδῶνος,

verses.english: who came to hear him and to be cured of their diseases; and those troubled by unclean spirits were being healed.
verses.greek: οἳ ἦλθον ἀκοῦσαι αὐτοῦ καὶ ἰαθῆναι ἀπὸ τῶν νόσων αὐτῶν· καὶ οἱ ἐνοχλούμενοι ἀπὸ πνευμάτων ἀκαθάρτων ἐθεραπεύοντο·

verses.english: And the whole crowd was seeking to touch him, because power was going out from him and curing all.
verses.greek: καὶ πᾶς ὁ ὄχλος ἐζήτει ἅπτεσθαι αὐτοῦ, ὅτι δύναμις παρ’ αὐτοῦ ἐξήρχετο καὶ ἰᾶτο πάντας.

verses.english: And he, lifting up his eyes to his learners, was saying, "Fortunate are the destitute, because theirs is the kingdom of God.
verses.greek: Καὶ αὐτὸς ἐπάρας τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς αὐτοῦ εἰς τοὺς μαθητὰς αὐτοῦ ἔλεγεν· Μακάριοι οἱ πτωχοί, ὅτι αὐτῶν ἐστιν ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ.

verses.english: Fortunate are those who hunger now, because you will be fed. Fortunate are those who weep now, because you will laugh.
verses.greek: μακάριοι οἱ πεινῶντες νῦν, ὅτι χορτασθήσεσθε. μακάριοι οἱ κλαίοντες νῦν, ὅτι γελάσετε.

verses.english: Fortunate are you when the humans hate you, and when they set you apart and reproach you and throw out your name as evil because of the son of the human.
verses.greek: Μακάριοί ἐστε ὅταν μισήσωσιν ὑμᾶς οἱ ἄνθρωποι, καὶ ὅταν ἀφορίσωσιν ὑμᾶς καὶ ὀνειδίσωσιν καὶ ἐκβάλωσιν τὸ ὄνομα ὑμῶν ὡς πονηρὸν ἕνεκα τοῦ υἱοῦ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου·

verses.english: Rejoice in that day and leap, for look, your wage is great in heaven; for their fathers were doing the same things to the prophets.
verses.greek: χάρητε ἐν ἐκείνῃ τῇ ἡμέρᾳ καὶ σκιρτήσατε, ἰδοὺ γὰρ ὁ μισθὸς ὑμῶν πολὺς ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ· κατὰ τὰ αὐτὰ γὰρ ἐποίουν τοῖς προφήταις οἱ πατέρες αὐτῶν.

verses.english: But woe to you, the rich, because you are holding your comfort in full.
verses.greek: πλὴν οὐαὶ ὑμῖν τοῖς πλουσίοις, ὅτι ἀπέχετε τὴν παράκλησιν ὑμῶν.

verses.english: Woe to you who have been filled up now, because you will hunger. Woe, those who laugh now, because you will mourn and weep.
verses.greek: οὐαὶ ὑμῖν, οἱ ἐμπεπλησμένοι νῦν, ὅτι πεινάσετε. οὐαί, οἱ γελῶντες νῦν, ὅτι πενθήσετε καὶ κλαύσετε.

verses.english: Woe when all the humans speak well of you, for their fathers were doing the same things to the false prophets.
verses.greek: Οὐαὶ ὅταν ὑμᾶς καλῶς εἴπωσιν πάντες οἱ ἄνθρωποι, κατὰ τὰ αὐτὰ γὰρ ἐποίουν τοῖς ψευδοπροφήταις οἱ πατέρες αὐτῶν.

verses.english: But to you I say, to those who are hearing: love your enemies, do good to those who hate you,
verses.greek: Ἀλλὰ ὑμῖν λέγω τοῖς ἀκούουσιν, ἀγαπᾶτε τοὺς ἐχθροὺς ὑμῶν, καλῶς ποιεῖτε τοῖς μισοῦσιν ὑμᾶς,

verses.english: bless those who curse you, pray for those who mistreat you.
verses.greek: εὐλογεῖτε τοὺς καταρωμένους ὑμᾶς, προσεύχεσθε περὶ τῶν ἐπηρεαζόντων ὑμᾶς.

verses.english: To the one who strikes you on the jaw, offer the other also; and from the one who takes away your cloak, do not withhold the tunic either.
verses.greek: τῷ τύπτοντί σε ἐπὶ τὴν σιαγόνα πάρεχε καὶ τὴν ἄλλην, καὶ ἀπὸ τοῦ αἴροντός σου τὸ ἱμάτιον καὶ τὸν χιτῶνα μὴ κωλύσῃς.

verses.english: To everyone who asks you, keep giving; and from the one who takes away what is yours, do not ask it back.
verses.greek: παντὶ αἰτοῦντί σε δίδου, καὶ ἀπὸ τοῦ αἴροντος τὰ σὰ μὴ ἀπαίτει.

verses.english: And just as you want the humans to do to you, do to them likewise.
verses.greek: καὶ καθὼς θέλετε ἵνα ποιῶσιν ὑμῖν οἱ ἄνθρωποι, ποιεῖτε αὐτοῖς ὁμοίως.

verses.english: And if you love those who love you, what kind of favour is that to you? For even the sinners love those who love them.
verses.greek: Καὶ εἰ ἀγαπᾶτε τοὺς ἀγαπῶντας ὑμᾶς, ποία ὑμῖν χάρις ἐστίν; καὶ γὰρ οἱ ἁμαρτωλοὶ τοὺς ἀγαπῶντας αὐτοὺς ἀγαπῶσιν.

verses.english: For indeed, if you do good to those who do good to you, what kind of favour is that to you? The sinners also do the same.
verses.greek: καὶ γὰρ ἐὰν ἀγαθοποιῆτε τοὺς ἀγαθοποιοῦντας ὑμᾶς, ποία ὑμῖν χάρις ἐστίν; καὶ οἱ ἁμαρτωλοὶ τὸ αὐτὸ ποιοῦσιν.

verses.english: And if you lend to those from whom you hope to receive, what kind of favour is that to you? Sinners too lend to sinners, so that they may receive back the equal amount.
verses.greek: καὶ ἐὰν δανίσητε παρ’ ὧν ἐλπίζετε λαβεῖν, ποία ὑμῖν χάρις ἐστίν; καὶ ἁμαρτωλοὶ ἁμαρτωλοῖς δανίζουσιν ἵνα ἀπολάβωσιν τὰ ἴσα.

verses.english: But love your enemies, and do good, and lend, despairing of nothing; and your wage will be great, and you will be sons of the Highest, because he is kind toward the ungrateful and evil.
verses.greek: πλὴν ἀγαπᾶτε τοὺς ἐχθροὺς ὑμῶν καὶ ἀγαθοποιεῖτε καὶ δανίζετε μηδὲν ἀπελπίζοντες· καὶ ἔσται ὁ μισθὸς ὑμῶν πολύς, καὶ ἔσεσθε υἱοὶ Ὑψίστου, ὅτι αὐτὸς χρηστός ἐστιν ἐπὶ τοὺς ἀχαρίστους καὶ πονηρούς.

verses.english: Become compassionate, just as your Father is compassionate.
verses.greek: γίνεσθε οἰκτίρμονες καθὼς ὁ πατὴρ ὑμῶν οἰκτίρμων ἐστίν·

verses.english: And do not judge, so that you may not be judged; and do not condemn, so that you may not be condemned. Release, and you will be released.
verses.greek: Καὶ μὴ κρίνετε, ἵνα μὴ κριθῆτε· καὶ μὴ καταδικάζετε, ἵνα μὴ καταδικασθῆτε. ἀπολύετε, καὶ ἀπολυθήσεσθε·

verses.english: Give, and it will be given to you: a fine measure, pressed down, shaken, pouring over, they will give into your fold. For by the same measure by which you measure, it will be measured back to you."
verses.greek: δίδοτε, καὶ δοθήσεται ὑμῖν· μέτρον καλὸν πεπιεσμένον σεσαλευμένον ὑπερεκχυννόμενον δώσουσιν εἰς τὸν κόλπον ὑμῶν· τῷ γὰρ αὐτῷ μέτρῳ ᾧ μετρεῖτε ἀντιμετρηθήσεται ὑμῖν.

verses.english: And he also said a parable to them: "Can a blind person lead a blind person? Will they not both fall into a pit?
verses.greek: Εἶπεν δὲ καὶ παραβολὴν αὐτοῖς· Μήτι δύναται τυφλὸς τυφλὸν ὁδηγεῖν; οὐχὶ ἀμφότεροι εἰς βόθυνον ἐμπεσοῦνται;

verses.english: A learner is not above the teacher; but everyone who has been fully trained will be like his teacher.
verses.greek: οὐκ ἔστιν μαθητὴς ὑπὲρ τὸν διδάσκαλον, κατηρτισμένος δὲ πᾶς ἔσται ὡς ὁ διδάσκαλος αὐτοῦ.

verses.english: Why do you look at the splinter in your brother's eye, but the beam in your own eye you do not consider?
verses.greek: τί δὲ βλέπεις τὸ κάρφος τὸ ἐν τῷ ὀφθαλμῷ τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ σου, τὴν δὲ δοκὸν τὴν ἐν τῷ ἰδίῳ ὀφθαλμῷ οὐ κατανοεῖς;

verses.english: How can you say to your brother, 'Brother, let me throw out the splinter in your eye,' when you yourself do not see the beam in your eye? Play-actor, first throw the beam out of your eye, and then you will see clearly to throw out the splinter in your brother's eye.
verses.greek: πῶς δύνασαι λέγειν τῷ ἀδελφῷ σου· Ἀδελφέ, ἄφες ἐκβάλω τὸ κάρφος τὸ ἐν τῷ ὀφθαλμῷ σου, αὐτὸς τὴν ἐν τῷ ὀφθαλμῷ σου δοκὸν οὐ βλέπων; ὑποκριτά, ἔκβαλε πρῶτον τὴν δοκὸν ἐκ τοῦ ὀφθαλμοῦ σου, καὶ τότε διαβλέψεις τὸ κάρφος τὸ ἐν τῷ ὀφθαλμῷ τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ σου ἐκβαλεῖν.

verses.english: For there is no fine tree producing rotten fruit, nor again a rotten tree producing fine fruit.
verses.greek: Οὐ γάρ ἐστιν δένδρον καλὸν ποιοῦν καρπὸν σαπρόν, οὐδὲ πάλιν δένδρον σαπρὸν ποιοῦν καρπὸν καλόν.

verses.english: For each tree is known by its own fruit; for they do not gather figs from thorns, nor do they harvest a bunch of grapes from a bramble.
verses.greek: ἕκαστον γὰρ δένδρον ἐκ τοῦ ἰδίου καρποῦ γινώσκεται· οὐ γὰρ ἐξ ἀκανθῶν συλλέγουσιν σῦκα, οὐδὲ ἐκ βάτου σταφυλὴν τρυγῶσιν.

verses.english: The good person brings out the good from the good treasure of the heart, and the evil one brings out the evil from the evil; for out of the overflow of the heart his mouth speaks.
verses.greek: ὁ ἀγαθὸς ἄνθρωπος ἐκ τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ θησαυροῦ τῆς καρδίας προφέρει τὸ ἀγαθόν, καὶ ὁ πονηρὸς ἐκ τοῦ πονηροῦ προφέρει τὸ πονηρόν· ἐκ γὰρ περισσεύματος καρδίας λαλεῖ τὸ στόμα αὐτοῦ.

verses.english: Why do you call me 'lord, lord', and do not do what I say?
verses.greek: Τί δέ με καλεῖτε· Κύριε κύριε, καὶ οὐ ποιεῖτε ἃ λέγω;

verses.english: Everyone who comes to me and hears my words and does them, I will show you whom he is like:
verses.greek: πᾶς ὁ ἐρχόμενος πρός με καὶ ἀκούων μου τῶν λόγων καὶ ποιῶν αὐτούς, ὑποδείξω ὑμῖν τίνι ἐστὶν ὅμοιος·

verses.english: he is like a person building a house, who dug and went deep and laid a foundation on the rock; and when a flood came, the river broke against that house, and was not strong enough to shake it, because it had been built well.
verses.greek: ὅμοιός ἐστιν ἀνθρώπῳ οἰκοδομοῦντι οἰκίαν ὃς ἔσκαψεν καὶ ἐβάθυνεν καὶ ἔθηκεν θεμέλιον ἐπὶ τὴν πέτραν· πλημμύρης δὲ γενομένης προσέρηξεν ὁ ποταμὸς τῇ οἰκίᾳ ἐκείνῃ, καὶ οὐκ ἴσχυσεν σαλεῦσαι αὐτὴν διὰ τὸ καλῶς οἰκοδομῆσθαι αὐτήν.

verses.english: But the one who heard and did not do is like a person who built a house on the ground without a foundation, against which the river broke, and at once it collapsed, and the breaking of that house became great."
verses.greek: ὁ δὲ ἀκούσας καὶ μὴ ποιήσας ὅμοιός ἐστιν ἀνθρώπῳ οἰκοδομήσαντι οἰκίαν ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν χωρὶς θεμελίου, ᾗ προσέρηξεν ὁ ποταμός, καὶ εὐθὺς συνέπεσεν, καὶ ἐγένετο τὸ ῥῆγμα τῆς οἰκίας ἐκείνης μέγα.

notes.explanation: Tertullian, Marc. 4.13.1–6: he went up the mountain and spent the night in prayer, chose twelve (with figures of the number from the Creator's scriptures), and named Simon Peter. Epiphanius, sch. 4: »Ἰούδαν Ἰσκαριώτην, ὃς ἐγένετο προδότης«. The other names are not cited. 6:14 is printed whole because the verse is attested; 6:15 is printed in grey. The previous text replaced 6:15 with ellipses (research question Q3c); that is superseded. On the form of Judas' surname: NA27 prints Ἰσκαριώθ and cites Marcion (McionE) for Ἰσκαριώτην, but that rests on Holl's emendation of Epiphanius; his manuscripts V and M read -ώθ. The NA27 form is kept. The previous note presented Ἰσκαριώθ as a Marcionite reading; it is withdrawn.

Epiphanius, sch. 4: instead of "coming down with them" the text had "he came down among them" (κατέβη ἐν αὐτοῖς). Tertullian, Marc. 4.13.6: "they gather from Tyre and other regions, a multitude even from across the sea", which agrees in sense with the reading καὶ τῆς περαίας of ℵ* W and ff2. Roth rates both as probable or possible; they are noted, not printed. Epiphanius, sch. 5 quotes 6:19a with the singular ἐζήτει, printed here (Roth: very likely; NA27 ἐζήτουν). 6:18 is not cited and is printed in grey.

notes.term: "Fortunate are the destitute, because theirs is the kingdom of God" (6:20)
notes.explanation: Tertullian, Marc. 4.14.1: "Beati mendici (sic enim exigit interpretatio vocabuli quod in Graeco est), quoniam illorum est regnum dei", repeated at 4.14.13. "Illorum" (theirs) cannot translate ὑμετέρα (yours). NA27 records αὐτῶν in W, the Old Latin ff2, the Old Syriac (sys) and the Sahidic, and cites Marcion (McionT). Roth: very likely. It is printed. Tertullian's blessing has no "in spirit". Epiphanius, sch. 5 attests 6:20a.

notes.term: The destitute as a named group
notes.explanation: Interpretation. In the third person the blessing describes a class of people, the destitute (οἱ πτωχοί), and assigns the kingdom to them; it is not only an address to the listeners. Paul's letters use the same word (οἱ πτωχοί, "the poor") for the Jerusalem community (Gal 2:10; Rom 15:26), and the Epistle of James says that God chose the poor of the world to be heirs of the kingdom (Jas 2:5) and pronounces woe on the rich (Jas 5:1; cf. Lk 6:24). Later writers name a Jewish-Christian group the Ebionites (from Hebrew ebyonim, "the poor"). The library identifies the community behind the text with that group (Carriers of Living Water §1). The attested wording of 6:20 is consistent with that identification. It does not prove it: the third person also stands in W, the Old Syriac and the Old Latin ff2.

Tertullian, Marc. 4.14.9–14 and 4.15.1; Epiphanius, sch. 6. Tertullian twice gives 6:21 in the third person and without "now" ("Beati esurientes, quoniam ipsi saturabuntur"; "Beati qui plorant, quoniam ridebunt"), and NA27 cites him for both. Roth rates these possible only, and the NA27 wording is printed. At 6:22 Tertullian lacks "and when they set you apart". 6:23c is quoted by both witnesses, but they differ on the pronoun: Epiphanius has "your fathers" and Tertullian "their fathers" (= NA27). The previous note said 6:23c was a later addition to the text; both witnesses contradict that, and the note is withdrawn.

Tertullian, Marc. 4.15.3–14; Eznik, De Deo 405 (via Roth). Tertullian argues at length that woe on the rich is the Creator's language, which shows the woes stood in Marcion's text. At 6:25 he has no "now" after "full", and at 6:26 no "all"; NA27 cites Marcion for both omissions, with A D and others at 6:25 and D L and others at 6:26. Each rests on one witness and is noted, not printed. At 6:26 NA27's order ὑμᾶς καλῶς is printed (SBLGNT has καλῶς ὑμᾶς).

Tertullian, Marc. 4.16.1–16; Adamantius (via Roth). Tertullian gives 6:27–28 as "love your enemies, and bless those who hate you, and pray for those who slander you". The previous text printed that compressed form, which Roth rates possible only; the NA27 wording is restored. At 6:29 Tertullian has the garments in Matthew's order. 6:30b is not cited. At 6:31 Tertullian's form is "as you wish it to be done to you by people, so you also do to them"; NA27 cites him for "you also". Only Tertullian attests it, and a Latin writer can recast the voice of a clause, so NA27 is printed (METHOD §5.4).

Tertullian, Marc. 4.17.1–10. 6:32–33 are not cited and are printed in grey (6:33 with NA27's bracketed [γάρ]); 6:34b and 6:35a are not cited. Three Marcionite readings are printed because the Latin cannot render the NA27 Greek and Greek manuscripts carry the same reading (NA27 cites Marcion each time). At 6:36 there is no "also" (καί), with ℵ B L W. At 6:37 Tertullian has "Nolite iudicare, ne iudicemini. Nolite condemnare, ne condemnemini" (ἵνα μή twice), with D W and the Old Latin and Old Syriac. At 6:38 "eadem qua mensi eritis mensura" gives "with the same measure" (τῷ γὰρ αὐτῷ μέτρῳ), with 𝔓45vid A C and the Byzantine text. At 6:34 Tertullian's "recepturos" can render NA27's λαβεῖν, so the text is unchanged.

Tertullian, Marc. 4.17.6, on 6:35b: "Well done, Marcion: you have cleverly taken the rain and the sun away from him, so that he would not look like the Creator." The rain and sun stand in Matthew 5:45, not in any text of Luke. In the same way Tertullian charges three times (4.7.4, 4.9.15, 4.12.14) that Marcion erased "I came not to destroy the law but to fulfil it", which is Matthew 5:17 and stands in no manuscript of Luke. These charges measure Marcion's text against Matthew. They are evidence of what Tertullian expected a gospel to contain, not of what Luke contained, and they are not used as reports of content (METHOD §2).

notes.term: Blind guides, the beam, the two trees, the two treasures (6:39–45)
notes.explanation: Tertullian, Marc. 4.17.11 cites these in sequence and turns them against Marcion, Cerdo and Apelles: "the blind leads the blind into a pit… a disciple is not above his master… let the heretic take the beam from his own eye… a good tree does not bear bad fruit… Marcion brought nothing good out of the evil treasure of Cerdo." 6:44 is not cited and is printed in grey. At 6:45 NA27 has no "his" after "heart" (SBLGNT adds αὐτοῦ).

notes.term: The two trees in Marcion's church
notes.explanation: Reception. Marcion's followers used 6:43 as their proof text for two gods, a good one and a just one (Origen, Princ. 2.5.4; Hippolytus, Haer. 10.19.3; cited via Roth; the library: Dancing with Fire). In the text the saying is applied to persons: 6:45 explains the fruit as what a person brings out of the treasure of the heart. Tertullian makes the same point ("which Christ applied figuratively to people, not to two gods", Marc. 4.17.12). The two-gods reading belongs to the community that kept the text, not to its wording.

Tertullian, Marc. 4.17.12–13 quotes 6:46: "Why do you call me Lord, Lord… and do not do what I say?" 6:47–49 (the two houses) are not cited and are printed in grey. Interpretation: the sermon ends on doing, not on confessing. The Epistle of James makes the same demand ("be doers of the word, and not hearers only", Jas 1:22), and the library sets the two side by side (Carriers of Living Water §3.4). Of the three parallels the library draws inside this sermon (6:24 / Jas 5:1; 6:37 / Jas 5:9; 6:46 / Jas 1:22), all three are attested for this text.

notes.term: τῇ προσευχῇ τοῦ θεοῦ, "the prayer of God"
notes.explanation: The genitive is usually taken as "prayer to God". The Greek says "the prayer of God", and it is kept.
With the article: "the mountain". As at 4:29, ὄρος covers hill and mountain.
One word: to pass the night through.
ἀπόστολος is one sent out, from ἀποστέλλω, "send" (4:43). "Apostle" is the Greek word left untranslated, which later became a church title.
Literally "one who is zealous". It can mean zealous for the law, or a member of the later Zealot party. Lower case, as a description.
The Greek gives only the genitive, "of Jacob": son or brother is not said. Ἰούδας is the name Judah.
The spelling of this text. The meaning of the name is not known; "man of Kerioth" is one proposal.
One who betrays, hands over.
From the mountain of 6:12.
The people as a nation, often Israel, as distinct from ὄχλος, "crowd".
Both verbs stand side by side here. They are kept apart as everywhere.
Singular with "the whole crowd": the reading of this text.
μακάριος describes a state of good fortune, of being well off. "Blessed" is the usual rendering, but it is the English for a different Greek word, εὐλογέω (6:28), and merges the two.
πτωχός is a beggar, someone with nothing, as distinct from πένης, someone poor who works. Tertullian insists that the word requires mendici, "beggars" (Marc. 4.14.1). "The poor" is too mild.
Third person in this text; canonical Luke has "yours".

notes.term: "those who hunger… you will be fed"
notes.explanation: The Greek moves from "those who" to "you" inside the sentence. The participle with the article can also be read as an address, "you who hunger".
χορτάζω, to feed to the full; it is used of feeding animals until they are full.
To mark off, separate, exclude.

notes.term: ἐκβάλωσιν τὸ ὄνομα, "throw out your name"
notes.explanation: The verb of 4:29 ("threw him out").
To leap, spring about.
Pay for work, wages. "Reward" softens it. Again at 6:35.
The imperfect: what they used to do.
A word of commerce: to have received payment in full and give a receipt.
Consolation, encouragement, comfort.
A perfect participle: filled full and staying full.
Literally "say finely of you".
ἀγαπάω is the ordinary Greek verb for loving. The idea that it names a special, divine kind of love is a later theological reading, not a feature of the word.

notes.term: τοῖς ἀκούουσιν, "to those who are hearing"
notes.explanation: The present participle: those who are listening now.
To speak well of, to bless. A different word from μακάριος, "fortunate" (6:20).
To abuse, insult, treat spitefully.
The jaw or cheek.
The outer garment and the one worn next to the skin.
A present imperative: give, and go on giving.
Goodwill, a gift given freely, and the thanks or credit that answers it. Here: what credit is there in it for you?

The usual sense of ἀπελπίζω is "to give up hope, despair". The common rendering "expecting nothing in return" reads it from ἐλπίζω in 6:34, "hope to receive". Both senses are possible. The ordinary one is kept.
A male plural, used of a whole group. The Greek word is kept.
A name for God, "the Most High". Capitalised as a name.
Good, useful, kind. In speech it sounded almost the same as χριστός, "anointed".
Literally "without favour" (χάρις, 6:32–34): those who give no thanks.
To come to be. The present imperative: keep becoming.
Feeling pity. It is not ἐλεήμων, "merciful", which the English often uses here.
The reading of this text: a purpose clause ("so that you may not be judged"). Canonical Luke has a promise ("and you will not be judged").
To set free, to discharge: a prisoner, a debtor. "Forgive" or "pardon" narrows it to one case.
καλός, fine, good to look at. It is kept apart from ἀγαθός, "good" (6:45).
An impersonal plural, "people will give". The Semitic way of speaking often uses it to avoid naming God.
The fold of the garment at the chest, used as a pocket. The same word is the "bosom" of Abraham (16:22).
Running over the brim.
A question that expects "no".
To put in order, make complete, mend. It is the verb used for mending nets.
A dry stalk or splinter, and a roof beam.
ἀφίημι, "let go, let": the verb of "let sins go" (5:20).
The verb of 4:29 and of driving out daimons.
ὑποκριτής is a stage actor, one who plays a part. "Hypocrite" is the Greek word left untranslated.
Kept as the Greek word, though it is used of fellow members of a community.
καλός is fine, sound. σαπρός is rotten, decayed.
ἀγαθός is good in itself. πονηρός is evil, malicious, worthless.
What is more than enough, the surplus.
The ordinary address to a master. In lower case, because it is not the divine name.
λόγος, as at 4:32.
From βάθος, "the deep" (5:4).
πέτρα is bedrock, a rock mass. Πέτρος (Peter, 6:14) is the masculine form, "a stone".
To dash against, break upon.
A breaking, a rupture. It is from ῥήγνυμι, "burst" (5:37).

chapters.title: Proto-Luke Chapter 4
chapters.preamble: Four scenes from the Galilean ministry. A centurion's faith is measured against Israel: "not even in Israel have I found such trust." A widow's only son is raised at Nain, and the crowd acclaims Jesus in the language of Israel's scripture: "A great prophet has been raised among us" and "God has visited his people." John the Baptist sends to ask whether Jesus is the one to come, and Jesus answers with the works of the prophets and calls John more than a prophet. In a Pharisee's house a woman of the town anoints his feet, and her sins are forgiven "because she loved much." Tertullian works through the chapter in order (Marc. 4.18) and Epiphanius quotes from four of the scenes. Not printed: the passage on John's baptism and "this generation" (7:29–35), which no witness cites although Tertullian's argument needed it.

verses.english: When he had completed all his sayings in the ears of the people, he went into Capernaum.
verses.greek: Ἐπειδὴ ἐπλήρωσεν πάντα τὰ ῥήματα αὐτοῦ εἰς τὰς ἀκοὰς τοῦ λαοῦ, εἰσῆλθεν εἰς Καφαρναούμ.

verses.english: And a certain centurion's slave, who was in a bad way, was about to come to his end; and he was valued by him.
verses.greek: Ἑκατοντάρχου δέ τινος δοῦλος κακῶς ἔχων ἤμελλεν τελευτᾶν, ὃς ἦν αὐτῷ ἔντιμος.

verses.english: Hearing about Jesus, he sent to him elders of the Judeans, asking him to come and bring his slave safely through.
verses.greek: ἀκούσας δὲ περὶ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ἀπέστειλεν πρὸς αὐτὸν πρεσβυτέρους τῶν Ἰουδαίων, ἐρωτῶν αὐτὸν ὅπως ἐλθὼν διασώσῃ τὸν δοῦλον αὐτοῦ.

verses.english: And when they came to Jesus, they were urging him earnestly, saying, "He is worthy that you should grant him this,
verses.greek: οἱ δὲ παραγενόμενοι πρὸς τὸν Ἰησοῦν παρεκάλουν αὐτὸν σπουδαίως λέγοντες ὅτι Ἄξιός ἐστιν ᾧ παρέξῃ τοῦτο,

verses.english: for he loves our nation, and he himself built the assembly for us."
verses.greek: ἀγαπᾷ γὰρ τὸ ἔθνος ἡμῶν καὶ τὴν συναγωγὴν αὐτὸς ᾠκοδόμησεν ἡμῖν.

verses.english: And Jesus was going with them. And when he was already not far from the house, the centurion sent friends, saying to him, "Lord, do not trouble yourself, for I am not fit for you to come in under my roof;
verses.greek: ὁ δὲ Ἰησοῦς ἐπορεύετο σὺν αὐτοῖς. ἤδη δὲ αὐτοῦ οὐ μακρὰν ἀπέχοντος ἀπὸ τῆς οἰκίας ἔπεμψεν φίλους ὁ ἑκατοντάρχης λέγων αὐτῷ· Κύριε, μὴ σκύλλου, οὐ γὰρ ἱκανός εἰμι ἵνα ὑπὸ τὴν στέγην μου εἰσέλθῃς·

verses.english: that is why I did not count myself worthy to come to you either. But say it with a word, and let my boy be cured.
verses.greek: διὸ οὐδὲ ἐμαυτὸν ἠξίωσα πρὸς σὲ ἐλθεῖν· ἀλλὰ εἰπὲ λόγῳ, καὶ ἰαθήτω ὁ παῖς μου·

verses.english: For I too am a person set under authority, having soldiers under myself; and I say to this one, 'Go!' and he goes, and to another, 'Come!' and he comes, and to my slave, 'Do this!' and he does it."
verses.greek: καὶ γὰρ ἐγὼ ἄνθρωπός εἰμι ὑπὸ ἐξουσίαν τασσόμενος, ἔχων ὑπ’ ἐμαυτὸν στρατιώτας, καὶ λέγω τούτῳ· Πορεύθητι, καὶ πορεύεται, καὶ ἄλλῳ· Ἔρχου, καὶ ἔρχεται, καὶ τῷ δούλῳ μου· Ποίησον τοῦτο, καὶ ποιεῖ.

verses.english: Hearing these things, Jesus marvelled at him, and turning to the crowd that was following him he said, "I tell you, not even in Israel have I found such trust."
verses.greek: ἀκούσας δὲ ταῦτα ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἐθαύμασεν αὐτόν, καὶ στραφεὶς τῷ ἀκολουθοῦντι αὐτῷ ὄχλῳ εἶπεν· Λέγω ὑμῖν, τοσαύτην πίστιν οὐδὲ ἐν τῷ Ἰσραὴλ εὗρον.

verses.english: And returning to the house, those who had been sent found the slave in health.
verses.greek: καὶ ὑποστρέψαντες εἰς τὸν οἶκον οἱ πεμφθέντες εὗρον τὸν δοῦλον ὑγιαίνοντα.

verses.english: And it happened on the next day that he journeyed to a city called Nain, and his learners and a large crowd were journeying with him.
verses.greek: Καὶ ἐγένετο ἐν τῷ ἑξῆς ἐπορεύθη εἰς πόλιν καλουμένην Ναΐν, καὶ συνεπορεύοντο αὐτῷ οἱ μαθηταὶ αὐτοῦ καὶ ὄχλος πολύς.

verses.english: And as he drew near to the gate of the city, look, a dead man was being carried out, the only-born son of his mother, and she was a widow; and a sizeable crowd of the city was with her.
verses.greek: ὡς δὲ ἤγγισεν τῇ πύλῃ τῆς πόλεως, καὶ ἰδοὺ ἐξεκομίζετο τεθνηκὼς μονογενὴς υἱὸς τῇ μητρὶ αὐτοῦ, καὶ αὐτὴ ἦν χήρα, καὶ ὄχλος τῆς πόλεως ἱκανὸς ἦν σὺν αὐτῇ.

verses.english: And seeing her, the lord was moved with compassion over her and said to her, "Do not weep."
verses.greek: καὶ ἰδὼν αὐτὴν ὁ κύριος ἐσπλαγχνίσθη ἐπ’ αὐτῇ καὶ εἶπεν αὐτῇ· Μὴ κλαῖε.

verses.english: And coming up, he touched the bier, and those carrying it stood still, and he said, "Young man, I say to you, get up!"
verses.greek: καὶ προσελθὼν ἥψατο τῆς σοροῦ, οἱ δὲ βαστάζοντες ἔστησαν, καὶ εἶπεν· Νεανίσκε, σοὶ λέγω, ἐγέρθητι.

verses.english: And the dead man sat up and began to speak, and he gave him to his mother.
verses.greek: καὶ ἀνεκάθισεν ὁ νεκρὸς καὶ ἤρξατο λαλεῖν, καὶ ἔδωκεν αὐτὸν τῇ μητρὶ αὐτοῦ.
